Day had broken cold and gray when the man turned off the main Yukon trail and climbed the high bank of the frozen river. <break time="0.8s" /> It was nine oclock, but there was no sun or hint of sun, and a strange gloom lay over the white land. <break time="0.8s" /> The strangeness of it all made no impression on the man, a newcomer in the land, for this was his first winter there. <break time="0.8s" /> Fifty degrees below zero meant eighty odd degrees of frost to him, and that fact seemed only cold and uncomfortable. <break time="0.8s" /> The trouble with him was that he had no imagination, so the cold never made him think about his own weakness as a human. <break time="0.8s" /> To test the cold, he spat, and the spit crackled sharply in the air before it could fall to the snow. <break time="0.8s" /> He knew that spit crackled on the snow at fifty below, so it was surely colder than that, but how much colder he did not know. <break time="0.8s" /> He was heading for an old claim on Henderson Creek, where the boys were already waiting, and he would be there by six oclock. <break time="0.8s" /> His lunch of biscuits was wrapped in a handkerchief and carried inside his shirt, against his bare skin, to keep it from freezing.

At the mans heels trotted a dog, a big gray husky that looked just like its brother, the wild wolf. <break time="0.8s" /> The dog knew by instinct that it was no time for traveling, for it was really seventy five degrees below zero. <break time="0.8s" /> It walked close behind the man and watched his every move, as if it expected him to stop and build a fire. <break time="0.8s" /> He walked carefully along the frozen creek, for he knew that some springs under the snow never froze, even in the coldest weather. <break time="0.8s" /> Once the dog broke through into the water, and the man pulled off his mitten to tear the ice from its feet. <break time="0.8s" /> He bared his fingers for less than a minute, but he was astonished at how quickly they became numb. <break time="0.8s" /> At half past twelve he reached the forks of the creek, where he stopped to eat his lunch. <break time="0.8s" /> But the ice around his mouth would not let him bite the biscuit, for he had forgotten to build a fire first. <break time="0.8s" /> He remembered the old timer on Sulphur Creek, who had told him how cold it could get, and he had laughed at him at the time. <break time="0.8s" /> So he built a small fire, and sitting by its warmth, he ate his biscuits while the dog lay happily near the flames.
